utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Let me greet everyone in this courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused. Today we have a witness to hear. As I indicated in a written statement, both the Defence and the Prosecution will have three hours. Furthermore, I would like to tell you that the Trial Chamber has issued a number of rulings these past few days. Yesterday two major rulings have been filed. One of them is related to the admission of the written statement made by an accused. The second decision is related to the 23 additional hours that we granted to the Prosecution in order for them to complete the presentation of their case. I would like to invite all of you to read these decisions related to these two topics. Furthermore, I'd like to tell the parties that there is bank holiday in October, the 24th of October. It's a Wednesday. Because of this -- because we should be sitting on Thursday the 25th of October, but I think it would be better for everyone if the Prosecution did not have any witnesses on the 25th of October in order to give a break for everyone, and even more so since at that time we will be in the final stretch of the of Prosecution case. That's a time when the Defence will have to get ready for the rest of the proceedings. Therefore, I'd like to invite the Prosecution not to have a witness testify on the 25th of October. As you know, for reasons beyond our control we were not able to sit two days this week, and the same will happen next week because next week, on Wednesday the 29th, we won't be sitting because other trials are taking place in the other courtrooms, in the courtrooms. Cases have to take turns in the courtrooms, and as a result we won't be sitting next Wednesday. Furthermore, I will immediately issue two oral rulings. The Trial Chamber would like to ask the Defence to give an oral response to the Chamber's legal officer in relation to protective measures that were requested on the 12th of June, 2007 for a witness referred to in an application for admission of evidence pursuant to Article 92 bis A and B, Rule 92 bis A and B, Ljubuski. I would like to ask you by the end of the day to tell the Chamber's legal officer what is your position with respect to this application for evidence. Second ruling: The Defence asked for additional time to respond to three motions. On the 21st of August, 2007, the Chamber received a joint motion by the Defence where the Defence asked to be granted additional time to be granted until the 8th of October, 2007 to respond to three motions of the Prosecution, the first one being application for admission of evidence pursuant to -- to Rule 92 bis A and B for Dretelj, Gabela, and others, dated 13th of August, 2007. Second Prosecution motion, application for admission of documentary evidence with respect to the Heliodrom, dated 15th of August, 2007. Third motion: Application for admission of documentary evidence with respect to Dretelj and Gabela, dated 21st of August, 2007. The Trial Chamber would like to remind the party that it has already granted additional time for several responses, namely by its oral decision of the 12th of July, 2007. Considering that the three above-mentioned motions that the Defence needs to respond to require a great deal of work, the Trial Chamber believes that additional time should be granted to the Defence. Having said that, the Trial Chamber believes that two additional weeks will be amply sufficient. As a result, pursuant to Rule 126 bis, the Trial Chamber partially grants the Defence motion and grants the Defence 14 additional days to file their responses to the three motions. Let me add that pursuant to Rule 126 bis, the Defence normally has 14 days to respond to a motion. We grant them two additional weeks. In other words, the Defence has now one month to respond to each one of these motions. We are now going to have the witness brought in for the hearing to be organised properly, we need the Prosecution to complete the examination-in-chief today, and the cross-examination will take place next time, because the witness will come back to be cross-examined next week. This is the way we are going to proceed today. Let me ask the usher to bring the witness in. Oh, yes. Mr. Karnavas, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Two points. First with respect to the -- the decision that was recently made with respect to the statement. I'm not going to comment on behalf of my colleagues because they represent their own clients, but it's my understanding that the statement comes in against all of the accused, they may wish to speak up on that, but we would be moving for certification, and because it is in French and we want to be precise in how we respond, we would ask some additional time, say for instance five days after it is fully translated into English to file our motion for certification for appeal of that particular decision. That's the first, and you may decide what to do with that, but primarily I want to speak with respect to something else that I find rather regrettable to speak about and rather disturbing. Last Friday there was a hearing where apparently -- you were presiding over that where Mr. Seselj indicated that I had been engaged in illegal activity, including smuggling. Now, I am told -- I saw a part of the transcript. I'm told that there was no reaction from the Bench. In other words, one could interpret that as being an acquiescence or appeasement to what Mr. Seselj was saying. Now, I'm not interested in responding to that (redacted) (redacted). I do not intend to do that. But I do expect that when such matters are being brought before a Presiding Judge in this particular trial where it affects my client because it affects my ability to advocate properly for the client, I expect the Trial Chamber either to ask for clarification or do what Judge May did on many occasions in Milosevic, and that is to turn the mic off. There are rules and procedures and everyone including Mr. Seselj has to comply with those rules and procedures. The Judge cannot allow that individual, albeit he might have the backing of one of the permanent members of the Security Council, Russia in particular, it's an open secret -- or I should say not secret, but it's been widely held that Russia is pressuring this Tribunal to give Seselj whatever he wishes, which may be the reason why it appears that this institution is rather bankrupt when it comes to finding ways of controlling that gentleman, but I think that when his goal, as he stated, is to undermine the integrity of this Tribunal, is attacking another lawyer who is representing someone else, a Croat, one of his -- a nation which he, during his period in his activities, in his admissions were against -- was against, that is a point in time where I must say something has to be done. Now, if, Your Honour, you would believe what Mr. Seselj said, and there may be individuals out there that believe that, but if you do indeed believe that, but then I have no choice but to ask for your immediate disqualification effectively as of this moment, to step down and let somebody else preside, because that means that I have been casted as a criminal, and I have been judged as such, and as a result Mr. Prlic cannot get a fair trial. If on the other hand, which is what I believe the case to be, you do not believe what Mr. Seselj said, then I think that Mr. Seselj must be publicly reprimanded and henceforth in any future proceedings you, as long as you preside in that case, need to control that gentleman. He is not afforded the opportunity, every time he comes into court, to disparage the Prosecution or Defence counsel or witnesses or individuals that have nothing to do with his case. He may represent himself, but he must conduct himself in accordance with all the rules and the procedures and the code of conduct that all lawyers must comply with. He is not above the law, and on behalf of my colleagues here who have been on the receiving end and on behalf of the an association whom I represent as a president, I say this institution has to protect the integrity of the Defence counsel. We are not punching bags. And individuals such as Seselj are not permitted to make gratuitous remarks whenever they feel like, however they feel like, with impunity. I regret to have to say this, but I must say on behalf of my client, because I am concerned that because of these sorts of remarks that went unanswered now I'm less of an advocate, less capable to put my case forward on behalf of Mr. Prlic. I care not for my reputation. I care for my client's rights, and my client has been affected by those remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas, for these observations. Yes, indeed during the last Status Conference in the Seselj case he made the statements you have mentioned. The Trial Chamber will consider the matter and will consider your submissions, the submissions you have made, and the Trial Chamber will consider whether any -- anything should be done as a result of this. Of course as a Pre-Trial Judge in that case, I'm in a position to ask Mr. Seselj to supplement his previous statement. That's all I can say at this stage. We'll now have the witness brought in. Yes, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask Your Honours to allow half an hour longer for this witness, because it is a complicated expert document, and if you could accord half an hour longer for the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll consider the matter once the examination-in-chief has been completed. We'll now have the witness brought in. We need IC numbers to be given to a number of documents. We'll do that before we bring the witness in. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Antoon van der Grinten and the following IC numbers have been allocated to them. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 635; the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number 636; the list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 637; the list submitted by 6D shall be given Exhibit number 638; the list submitted by OTP in -- concerning the witness Larry Forbes shall be given Exhibit number 639; the list submitted by 3D concerning the same witness shall be given IC 640; and the list submitted by 5D concerning Larry Forbes shall be given IC number 641. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, could I ask you to stand up. Could you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ewa Tabeau. I'm born 26th of April, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a demographer. I'm working at the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, have you ever testified in other cases in this Tribunal? If that's the case, in which trials have you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I testified in this Tribunal at several cases. I testified in cases such as Slobodan Milosevic, Dragomir Milosevic. I have here a list of cases. In -- in Stakic, indeed, and in other cases, several other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you be testifying in other cases in the near future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I am aware right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm going to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. Madam, I'm going to give you a few explanations, but I will be short because you're a member of the OTP so you're familiar with the way we proceed here. Furthermore, you've already been examined and cross-examined. As a result all the information I could give you, you already know. You will first answer questions put to you by Mr. Stringer. That will take place today. And next week you will be answering to the questions put to you by the Defence as part of the cross-examination, and also to questions put to you by one of the accused, because I think one of the accused wants to put questions to you. That's what I wanted to tell you. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. As the Trial Chamber knows, we will be presenting three expert reports prepared by Ms. Tabeau as well as some of her -- or together with some of her colleagues in the Office of the Prosecutor Demographic Unit, and the intent or the hope is that we'll be able to do that most efficiently and hopefully in a way that's most clear for everyone by way of a PowerPoint presentation that's been made by Ms. Tabeau and me working together, and hopefully those have -- those slides have been distributed to all counsel, Defence counsel, as well as the Judges and in the booths to assist everyone's understanding of the testimony, so hopefully all of you have those in front of you. As well, we've loaded the PowerPoint presentation on our computer, and I will ask that the technical people if they can put it on the video screen so that I can follow along myself, and there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, just starting with the first page of the presentation, the slide, there's reference here to three reports that you'll be addressing during the course of your testimony, and before we talk about those I would like then to ask you just to give us a little bit of a summary or a resume of your education, your educational background in the field of demographics and then we'll talk a little bit more about some of work that you've done in that field as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have one question. Are we supposed to see the presentation in -- on the screen as well or we don't?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You should -- everyone should be seeing it. It may be --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Push the button there.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have the presentation and the transcript at the same time or is it possible or not? Sorry for this disruption. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the benefit of all, at the top of this slide you'll see a reference to the exhibit and the annex, and we'll be doing this throughout the presentation, Your Honours. The slides will refer to specific parts of the reports so that you can refer back to the reports if you wish.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I'd like to make an observation. I highly regard this approach by my colleagues of the Prosecution trying with the PowerPoint tool to improve the quality of the presentation and to assist those are listening, but we cannot forget that the accused have the right to receive it in their own language. I know that it will be simultaneously interpreted but it won't be the same because a PowerPoint is in fact a precis, a summary of the testimony, although it is a tool of course, but it is a summary of sorts, and it would be a good idea if that were to be prepared in Croatian. I don't know whether a Croatian version or copy exists or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is a presentation and here we have a page related to the education of the witness, we can see that the witness studied in Warsaw. No need to understand English to -- to see what it's all about. And then the questions that will be put to the witness will serve to understand what's on the screen. Please proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, could you give us a brief resume of your educational and professional background in the field of demographics?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As I said I'm a demographer. I studied and graduated statistics and econometrics. I come from Poland and studied in Warsaw at the Warsaw School of Economics. In 1991 I obtained my Ph.D in mathematical demography there. In 1981, I obtained my masters degree in econometrics and statistics. As part of my education I would also like to mention several scientific internships that I completed. I spent some time in the 90s, mid-90s is in the French National Demographic Institute. I also visited the German National Demographic Institute, and most recently in July, I had the opportunity to participate in a course given by epidemiologists on public health in human emergency situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Tabeau, if I could just ask you to slow down just a little bit so that the interpreters can work more accurately.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. At this course, I also had the opportunity to lecture in relation to issues of measurement and analysis of conflict deaths. I now work at the Office of the Prosecutor. I am the project leader of the Demographic Unit at the Office of the Prosecutor, and I have been doing this since September 2000. Before I spent almost nine years in the Dutch National Demographic Institute where I was conducting research on mortality and public health issues, and longevity for countries such as the Netherlands and other Western European countries, but also Central and Eastern European countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just jump in there and ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but on the first page the degrees the witness obtained are described as "with honours", I think, and I would just like to know whether this would correspond to "cum laude" in the traditional academic qualifications or whether it is a different qualification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time in the system we had in Poland "with honours" had the meaning of obtaining the highest grade which at the time was the 5. That was the best possible, and this is what I achieved in both cases, but the cum laude as such was not explicitly used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now Ms. Tabeau, moving to the next slide that's on the screen there are references to expert testimonies that you've given in other cases here at the Tribunal as well as expert reports that have been submitted in additional cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. I already mentioned cases such as Slobodan Milosevic, Dragomir Milosevic, General Galic, Stakic. I testified twice in Stakic. I also testified in -- in the Simic et al., that is a case related to Bosanska Posavina. And in Lukic. There were several more reports. I didn't have testimonies in relation to the other reports, but the reports were used -- submitted, tendered into evidence and used in the other cases as well, altogether more than 20 reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we will talk about this in some greater detail later, but in general, can you tell us whether methods of analysis, sources of data that you used to make the reports in this case are similar or correspond to those that you've used in other cases in which you've appeared as an expert?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The methods, sources and approaches that we've been using in all these cases are similar. Worth mentioning is perhaps the approach we've been using for the quantification of the numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees. This approach has been used many years now, and it was presented in several cases. We originally prepared these statistics for use in the Slobodan Milosevic case where we presented an expert report with the same type of statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I've moved to the next slide which has a reference to some of your more latest projects, and there are references here to publications that have appeared in the scholarly journals within your profession, and those publications relate in part at least to the work that you've been doing here at the Tribunal, and I simply wanted to ask you whether in your own field whether the work that you've been doing here has been received favourably within the field of the demography that you're engaged in.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These titles that are shown right now on the screen are a few latest achievements. They are all related to the quantitative analysis of demographic consequences of conflict, mainly these papers are related to the casualties, to the killed persons in relation to conflict, as consequence of conflict. I certainly believe that several of these publications had a lot of impact in the field, but also on public opinion. We, at some point, published an article together with Jakub Bijak in which we discussed the number of war casualties in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe this particular paper certainly had a lot of impact in terms of both the method, the approach we applied, the sources we applied, but also the result that is obtained and presented in this paper. Another publication is a book which I edited with Helge Brunborg and Henrik Urdal. Helge Brunborg used to work at OTP demographic before I worked here and Henrik Urdal also spent some time working on this project. We know each other from the past and the book is a collection of articles that were presented at a seminar organised by -- by a working group of which we are all members, and this working group is called, right now, the scientific panel of -- on demography of conflict. I believe it is an important working group that is a leading group of researchers in demography in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these are the three reports now appearing on the screen, the first of which is a report that you and your colleagues made in respect of ethnic composition, internally displaced persons and refugees from eight municipalities of Herceg-Bosna, and after we talk about that, we'll move on then to additional reports or studies that you did that related to siege of East Mostar, killed persons, and wounded persons during the course of those months in 1993 in East Mostar. I can skip over this slide because I think we've already touched on this. The fact that at least with respect to -- well, in addition, I should say, to the study, the work that's been done on wounded and killed in a siege situation, the methods that you're going to be talking about in respect of your demographic studies of refugees and IDPs from these municipalities, those same methods and sources have been used by you in these additional cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. The results come from one project made for the case of Slobodan Milosevic and statistics are all consistent throughout all these cases. So are the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now focusing on the first of the studies that relates to IDPs and refugees, just keying off this slide Ms. Tabeau in general can you tell us what was the subject or objectives in performing this specific study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is a study of population movements, of migration that we should see as forced migration, both internal and external, and in the context of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it's important to note that population migration is the major consequence of the conflict as the size of this migration, during and at the end of the conflict, was enormous. More than 50 per cent of the original census pre-conflict population was displaced externally or internally. So measurement of migration as a consequence of conflict is a very important issue. At the same time, it is very hard to find sources that could be used for this kind of work. Sources of migration especially from the conflict period are not possible to obtain. There is no statistical data, individual data that would include personal information about the migrants that could be used for this kind of study. This is why a different type of approach has to be applied to measure the migration. We used the approach which, in order to quantify the numbers of migrants in our approach, we compare the population at the outbreak of the conflict with the population at the end of the conflict, and we compare place of residence of this population whether it remained the same or changed during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on this slide there's a reference under the first point to eight municipalities and could you tell us please just what was the geographical, if you will, universe in which you were operating for purposes of this particular study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We used as a study area the area of eight municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The municipalities are listed on the slide. It was Capljina, Gornji Vakuf, Jablanica, Ljubuski, Mostar, Prozor, Stolac, and Vares. It is not that these eight municipalities we considered to be the Herceg-Bosna area. This is our study area which belongs to a larger area called Herceg-Bosna, but for this particular report we called these eight municipalities the Herceg-Bosna area, but these two issues shouldn't be confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then we'll talk in greater detail about the sources. There were three general sources; is that correct, for this study the population census from 1991 and then OSCE voter registers from 1997, 1998, and then thirdly registration of IDPs and refugees that was begun by UNHCR and then continued by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. These are the three sources that we used. It is very obvious right now that the sources are dated not necessarily as the indictment period is defined. We deal here with a broader period starting in March 1991, which gives us a measurement of the population at the outbreak of the conflict and at the other end we have the voters registration from 1997, 1998, and one additional source that is dated as of the year 2000. Well, we have good reasons that we actually used these sources, and -- well, first reason was that sources that could be covering exactly the indictment period don't exist. There is nothing that could be used for this kind of analysis as presented here. So the best we can get is on one hand the 1991 census and on the other hand is the voters registration 1997, 1998, and this is what we use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And on that again we're going to discuss these in greater detail but when you say these are the best you can get, given that that is the best, are these sources and the data contained in these sources nonetheless, did they provide you with a sufficient basis to do this study under the rules and practices that would be acceptable within the field of statistics and demographics?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the answer is certainly yes, although I must here note that sources that are used in human emergency situations, and conflict is certainly part of this human emergencies, perhaps the most important part, sources used in analysis of human emergency situations are not necessarily of the same quality and the same standard as sources used in, for instance, official statistics. There are very good reasons for this but in this particular case we shouldn't be complaining at all, because the population census is the best source of information about the population in any country. It is a complete population survey covering many aspects of the population and including a lot of individual details, including names and date of birth and father's name and place of birth and place of residence and ethnicity and religion and socio-economic variables and marital status and the children ever born and professional area is covered, et cetera, et cetera. So the census is an excellent source. Well, the beginning for our approach is excellent. On the other hand, we used voters registration. Voters registration is not a source that would be used by professional statisticians and official statistics. Nevertheless for our purposes for comparison with the census, this source is fairly satisfactory and can be used in the analysis as those presented in these reports. Not to mention the importance and value high value of the last source, the registration, official registration of internally displaced persons and refugees. This is also a very good source developed by -- very professionally and up to a high standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now there's a reference here to methods and I think I'm going to skip that now because we're going to address it in greater details as we get closer to your findings. Just to give some attention to the geographical area that you've described, we're looking at a map now and this will contain shaded municipalities. Are these the shaded municipalities here are the municipalities that form the basis of your study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. These are the eight municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And at this point I think it's necessary for us to address the issue of the boundaries of the municipalities and how they changed from this time in 1991 to 1997 and 1998, which is sort of the back end of your study after the Dayton agreement, and so I'm going to move from this slide to the next one, and perhaps you could just describe for us what we're seeing in this next slide here with these greater number of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. First of all what is marked with colour on this map is exactly the same what we have just seen on the previous map. What is different is the number of municipalities shown, and in several cases the municipal borders are different as well. On the previous map we saw pre-conflict municipalities. There were 109 of them in Bosnia. This is that map, yes. And on the next map we see many more municipalities, and in addition to this a red line splitting the country into two political entities. This part is -- is the part of Republika Srpska located at the eastern border with Serbia and in the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the rest of the country is the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: And our study area is mainly located in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, and on that point because it's one that affects the counting that comes later, we went -- is it correct to say, then, that we're going from eight pre-conflict or pre-Dayton municipalities to 14 post-Dayton municipalities within what had been the original eight and that the only two affected municipalities are Mostar, which was divided in, as part of the Dayton agreement, into a number of smaller municipalities, and then also Stolac which was divided into two municipalities, one of which remained or is part of the federation and then the eastern half being -- falling within the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it is basically the case only that the eight pre-war municipalities became not 14 but 16 post-war municipalities. Fourteen of them are in the federation area and two of them are in the area of Republika Srpska. And the two is one part of Stolac, Stolac-Berkovici it is called, and the other one which is composed of three small pieces is the Mostar-Srpski Mostar. And the rest, the 14 municipalities to the left of the Dayton line are in the federation area. So we will be basically speaking -- I will be basically speaking about changes in the 14 municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So we're going to be talking about eight municipalities, pre-Dayton, that became 14 municipalities post-Dayton?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, may I have one remark. So the major change introduced by the Dayton peace agreement is that a number of municipalities were split between the federation and the Republika Srpska and population movements in the split municipalities were related to the fact that Bosnian Serbs were moving from the federal area to the RS area and mainly Bosnian Muslims were moving from the RS area to the area of the federation. There were also some other changes. Some municipalities within the federation, like Vlasenica for instance, were also divided in two and some other municipalities, but right now these are less important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that's the geographical area and how it changes or the boundaries change pre-conflict and post conflict. Now you've already discussed the census, and perhaps using this slide you could very briefly - because I do want to keep going rather swiftly through this part - tell us more about the census, what kind of data it provided, the quality of the data that you found in the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I said the census is the most complete population survey. The principle of the census is to measure the population at a given moment of time. It is for statistical authority probably the most important and organisationally the most difficult and most challenging project. The census is conducted once per 10 years in most countries. It's a population census but in the case here of Bosnia and Herzegovina not only population but also households, dwellings, and agriculture were part of the census. Census is conducted -- census is conducted by using a questionnaire. A questionnaire is always prepared very carefully. It is -- in the former Yugoslavia it was a standardised questionnaire that was largely identical in all republics. The republics had the right to add some questions. Not all republics used this opportunity, but the core information was identical for every republic. The questionnaire included questions as those I mentioned earlier related to personal information, to place of birth, place of residence, et cetera. I don't want to repeat. The questionnaire is extensive and gives a very detailed picture of every individual registered in the census. The information is collected or was collected, we are speaking of 1991, in face-to-face interviews. The group of interviewers employed in the census was very large. These were several thousand of interviewers who were going and talking to people and collected this information. Of course the interviewers were prepared to do so because they were offered intensive and extensive training on how to do that. There were also guidelines printed in advance and distributed among interviewers and instructors, municipal instructors and republican instructors in advance, that data would be collected consistently, that the reporting would be uniform across the country. Well, the preparation of the census and the conduct of censuses is a long talk and I don't want to go into details of that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's largely found in annex B of your report --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, so the result being and let me then make a couple points and ask you to comment on them, the result was that data was obtained as to 4.4 million individuals in the entire country, Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991. You make reference to some of the deficiencies in the data, in the census, and there is a distinction between agriculture, dwelling and population data that I'd like you to address, and then finally briefly if you can just describe for us how you dealt with deficiencies that you found in the data.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. First my comment on the size. Yes, indeed, approximately 4.4 million records related to individuals residing in Bosnia as of 31st of March, 1991, was collected in the census. Regarding the deficiencies, indeed there are deficiencies, some deficiencies, this the census. Here I want to say there is no survey and no census anywhere else that is error free. This is impossible. Every survey conducted, whether large or small, includes errors. So it is not that the Bosnian census or census in Bosnia and Herzegovina is exceptional. It has certain deficiencies but the deficiencies can be dealt with in ways that prevent producing biased results. Well, the major deficiency from the point of view of our work comparing individual data from before the conflict with from after the conflict, what is most important is the personal information about individuals. Personal information includes names on the first place. Names contain spelling mistakes, and the spelling mistakes are related to the fact that the census material wasn't computerised. By using data entry it was scanned and therefore spelling mistakes related to the optical character recognition method used in the scanning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to be clear on that that's when a computer programme tries to read writing and then to assign an electronic or a digital character to that handwriting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, this is one deficiency. There are also other problems with the census. For instance, duplicates is an issue, although duplicates were checked and eliminated by the statistical authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Not all duplicates were eliminated. We additionally checked whether we could identify more and we did. These are -- these were not big numbers, marginal numbers. Another deficiency is that the usual checking of the survey material and census in particular is not only the checking of the completeness of the census and elimination of the duplicates from the census. One more step is the so-called logical control, that is, relationship between different data items reported for one the same person in the census questionnaire. The logical control in the 1991 census for Bosnia and Herzegovina was completed for the population part of the census but it wasn't completed for the agriculture and dwelling. So actually from our point of view, this is not a big issue because what we use is the population data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You didn't rely on the agriculture or dwelling data?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the population data that you contained was completed or was --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, again, very briefly how did you handle these deficiencies? What did you do to overcome them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we invested a lot of time and effort in correcting spelling mistakes in the names. For this purpose we -- we had run three different projects. We, first of all, used computer programmes that checked the spelling of the names and identified impossible combinations of letters, impossible in the Bosnian language, and names with these combinations were checked by native B/C/S speakers who corrected these impossible combinations by replacing them with possible combinations. Another method was that we compiled a table, a data table with names, complete names, first names, and surnames, and native B/C/S speakers were checking these names and proposing viable names for the names that didn't exist in the B/C/S language. And finally in the third project we used a household method to correct the names. Well, household information is available in the census so we were able to check within every household the names reported. And if within households correct names were reported, then all other incorrect names were replaced by the correct names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just so we're clear because we've talked about how this data has been used in other trials, what you're talking about here for the 1991 census was that done for just the eight municipalities in this report or has it been done for the entire country?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, it was done for the entire country, for the entire census, and it took us several years to improve the names, to correct the spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: There were several persons working on this project, B/C/S native speakers, who were studying and correcting the results from our computer programmes. There were people who were -- who wrote these programmes, people who had the necessary IT background in order to make this kind of work happen, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Tabeau, I've moved to the next slide because this is sort of the point that I'd like for you to address because you've identified deficiencies in the data or the census and I'd like for you to give us your overall impression of the quality or reliability of the data for purposes of your study?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As I said there were some deficiencies in the census but many of them have been improved, corrected. Not only spelling mistakes but also some other data problems like inconsistent -- inconsistent date of birth or some other issues of this kind. I believe that data problems in the census do not discredit this source as an excellent source of information about the pre-conflict population in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I don't think it is only my opinion. Well, the statistical authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina published several bulletins and they also published this data in statistical yearbooks. Authority, statistical authority of Croatia, also published the census data for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I believe the fact of publishing these results is -- is obvious, right? The publication would never take place if the quality of the source and deficiencies would be unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And for purposes of your report and your testimony in this case, can the census be reliably used in producing the statistics and the figures that you've provided in your report in this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I certainly believe it can be used in this kind of study.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next slide is -- we're going to talk about the census in relation to the eight municipalities of Herceg-Bosna that you've -- you've described, and with this slide could you just tell us what the numbers are. What are the census figures in respect of these eight pre-Dayton municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. We speak of -- of the population in eight municipalities, eight -- in the eight Herceg-Bosna municipalities in 1991 being 281.366 persons. This is the entire population in these municipalities including the children, as well as those at older ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now let me stop you there. That's the population of all persons who were living in these municipalities at the time the census was taken in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now the next point has a smaller number of those individuals as people who were born before 1980, and I'm going to ask you about this a little more later, but is that -- does that have to do with, then, the voting age of the people who were actually people who were old enough to vote in 1997, 1998, when you were then examining the other data, the OSCE voter registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. The age those born before 1980 of course has to do with the age of being eligible to vote. Well, for the 1997-8 we could only use the voters registers. That means only a group of the population. So in order to compare two things that are comparable we had to adjust the census population, and from the census we had to study only those born before a certain year, 1980 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So then to the third point. This 231.610 figure, this is sort of the starting point of your -- of your study group for purposes of your report then?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the study population which is coming from these eight municipalities shown right now on the map. This is the population born before 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about the second source in a little more detail, the voters registers from OSCE. This provides us with the ending point or the sort of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I am trying to follow the answers given by the witness, but I would like to make sure that I understand something. Madam, when you talk, we are under the impression that the entire census that was carried out that you were the one carrying out the census. I am slightly confused, because in your sources you talk about the 1991 census, the statistics of the former Yugoslavia, and they had taken 4.4 million people in order to carry out the census. The charts that are in your document, these charts are your own charts, aren't they, or are those charts that belong to the official statistics office for the year of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very good question. Well, I want to stress that the 1991 census was conducted by the statistical authority of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is a source that comes from Bosnia and Herzegovina, was compiled there by the statistical office in Sarajevo. We do have a copy of the census data. We not only have aggregate statistics from the census as those published by the statistical authorities at several occasions. We do have individual census records for every individual reported in the census. So we are able to use this individual data to compile our own statistics. When having individual data, we are able to make a selection or take a group from the census and analyse this group. This is what we did in this project. We took a group of the census records. The group was the individuals born before 1980, and we studied this group and compared this group with information that we had about the same people from other sources. So in fact we can summarise this as follows: We do use an official source, that is the census, but because of having access to individual census records we are in the position to compile any statistics that we need for this or other projects. So in my reports -- reports, charts, maps, data tables, even though the source is mentioned, the 1991 population census for Bosnia and Herzegovina, these statistics were compiled in my unit, in the demographic unit here at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I understand better. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify or to follow up on the president's question, you were not -- you were not personally involved in the gathering of the census data in 1991, were you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you received all of the census data from the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then -- and then you've given us the number of 4.4 million people. That's roughly or approximately the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina as of 1991 according to the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As of 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Approximately 4.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then bringing that number of 4.4 million down to the eight municipalities that are the subject of this report, how many people of those -- from 4.4 million we're going to come down to a number that's going to be the beginning point of your survey or your report, and what's that number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For me, it is the number 231.610.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is the study population from the population census for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again, that's the population of -- your study population from these eight municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Moreover it is not the entire population; only those born before 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's right. And the reason you've excluded people born before 1980 relates then to this next source; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right. It is related to the voters registers from the 1997 municipal election and 1998 parliamentary elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what did you use this source for?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This source is used in our project to compare with the population census. We used this source in order to study whether or not place of residence of individuals listed in the '91 census changed when observed in the period of '97, '98.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you right there because I just want to -- so we're clear. This is a source that you used to study whether or not a person's place of residence changed from 1991 to this time, 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And this OSCE voters registration, did this cover people who were living in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as people who were living in neighbouring countries in 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is a register of all voters eligible to vote. It covers people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and people from Bosnia and Herzegovina but living at the time of elections in other countries, in neighbouring countries, in the area of the former Yugoslavia, but also in other countries, in Western European countries and even other countries. So it is the basis for the establishing of the voters registers, especially the register of 1997, was actually the population reported in the 1991 population census. The lists of voters eligible to vote were made based on the names reported in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: And even technically speaking, electronic files from the census were used for the voters registration in 1997-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So OSCE actually used the 1991 census data to facilitate making these voter lists in 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Of course, it was possible to add new names if a person was not reported in the census, and there were a few cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: But, basically, it is the 1991 census population later used in the electoral lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So now on this slide you make reference to these two lists which were then merged into a single list which you used, and I'm going to move to the next slide then and just ask you to talk about how then you used this merged list of voters registration to come down to a number that you used again to track the people who had moved or who had stayed in those eight municipalities from 1991.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The voters registration -- the combined voters registration we combined these voters registers because it was important for us to include in our post-conflict sources as many names of survivors as possible. We merged these two sources by taking the 1997 register as the primary source and expanded this source by adding records of new voters registered in 1998. So it is basically the population of 1997 that is reported in the merged sources here in the merged voters registers. Well, the voters registers do not contain all the information from the census. They only contain personal information of individuals, but the personal information, this is what we actually need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As this together with the municipality where the voters register gives us the information that is needed to study in this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move to the next slide and ask you then to just bring it then down to the level of these eight municipalities, the information that turns out to be the most useful to you from the voters registration, how that relates then to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the first observation is that the size of the merged 1997-'98 voters register is approximately 2.700.000 individuals. This is of course much less than 4.4 million individuals registered in the census. But first of all this is because of the age groups covered by the voters register. Voters register is just a smaller group. But secondly, not all individuals eligible to vote registered to vote and participated in the elections. So there is a group that is not in the register at all. So this is another reason that we don't see it here. So, for 1997-8, we don't speak of a complete population of record of -- of the complete population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have a huge sample of this population registered. For the eight municipalities, this means quite some -- quite different numbers. Registered voters who registered in the eight Herceg-Bosna municipalities accounted to 145.061 voters. This is the first statistic. This is what we have for the eight Herceg-Bosna municipalities. Now, when we want to show the voters who registered in 1997 and 8, and at the same time were reported in the population census in the same eight municipalities, this group is slightly smaller. It is 142.204 voters. And this is a very important group, very important group. This is the group that will be -- is studied in our report. Once again I would like to repeat. These 142.000, approximately, voters are individuals who registered to vote in the 1997-1998 elections, but at the same time they were reported in the eight Herceg-Bosna municipalities in the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that what we've got now are 142.204 people, and you know where each of those persons are in 1997, 1998, and you also know where each of those people were in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So then is your study then looking at the differences in the composition of the people, where they lived in 1991 versus where they were found or where they were living in 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is actually the basic principle of our approach. We have a starting population, pre-conflict population that is population census for eight municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: And we traced this population in other sources and of the approximately 231.000 in 1991 we were able to find in the voters register 142.000, approximately, individuals. These are same individuals in both sources. We have the names of these individuals, other details of these individuals. We have place of residence of these individuals in 1991 and also we know for these individuals where they registered to vote whether in their home municipalities or in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, so that you know if someone who lived in Jablanica, for instance, someone living in Jablanica in 1991, for these 142.000 or so, you're able to tell where that person was living when he registered to vote in 1997 whether he was in Jablanica or in Stolac or in Germany?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we are able to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll talk more about that matching process, but let's move to the third source because, and I don't want to spend too much time on this, because I know in the next slide it's an indication that this is a sort of subsidiary source, but if you could describe this displaced persons and refugees database and what use you made of it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: As you said, it is a subsidiary resource. We looked at it for contextual purposes once we produced our statistics on displaced persons and refugees. In this case, displaced persons in particular. We wanted to check whether sources like the registration, official registration, of internal displacement showed similar statistics or similar geographic patterns. So our purpose was just contextual. We didn't use this sort for producing any statistics in our report. It is an important source, though, I must admit. It reports internal displacement and refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It contains people -- records of people who acquired the legal status of an internal -- internally displaced person or refugee. These records are important in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because they offer a basis for applications for compensations for the property lost. So this is a very good source, basically speaking, only that it is reporting the data as of the year 2000, which is even more distant from the conflict period than what we used in our study.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I moved to the next slide in which you indicate that this was a subsidiary source, it served as a reference for the OSCE statistics only on IDPs. I think with that actually we can move to the next slide. You made reference to this marching of names from 1997, 1998 to the names from the census data from 1991. Tell us about how the extent of matching, the level of matching that you were able to accomplish as between these two sources.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Perhaps it's important to explain a little bit what the matching stands for. Matching and what I earlier said, tracing records of a group of individuals in other sources is actually one the same thing. The idea of matching is checking whether or not a given record from a given source is also reported in another source. The method of matching is a well-recognised standard in social sciences, and especially in Scandinavian countries this method has been used for many years with a great degree of success. In the developed countries like the Scandinavian countries, matching is done easily on the basis of individual identification numbers reported for persons in sources through comparing these numbers. These are just numeric characteristics, it's easy to conclude records the same, into different sources or in more sources. Matching does not necessarily have to be conducted exclusively on the basis of numeric characteristics of individuals reported in the records. Matching can be done also on the basis of non-numeric characteristics like names, other personal information reported, including date of birth, place of birth, place of residence, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you there the matching process or the method that you used in this study, is it a process or analysis that is accepted and used more generally or would it be an accepted practice in the field of statistics and demography?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It certainly is but it is much more than statistics and social sciences or demography only. Matching has been used -- used by institutions like life insurances, health insurances, tax offices. Statistical authorities of countries use matching to increase the quantity of information about individuals. Well, it's important to understand that in many countries we don't have the population census as such at all. All the information about the population comes, first of all, from population register, which is matched or other term that is often used, linked with additional sources of information. Depending on the needs in developed countries, we can produce any statistics on the population, and it is only a beginning to have the population register. Having the register and individual identification numbers, it is a common practice nowadays to increase the information about individuals in any required way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, one the point here in the middle of the page, you indicate that 80 per cent of those in the voter register were matched with individuals found in the 1991 census. Is that a high or low matching level for your needs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as compared to what, Your Honour? As compared to what, this 80 per cent? I think the question needs to be rephrased. And I would go back also to the previous -- answer to the previous question. Matching methods that she used, the particular ones, are these the ones accepted within the scientific community, not in general whether matching is, but when -- when -- the question -- the question 80 per cent for her needs, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can clarify that question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Those are usually questions that should be put during the cross-examination, but, yes, you may ask for some precision, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you heard --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- counsel's comment. Would you like to address it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it is 80 per cent of records in the voters register that have been matched with the census. Well, whether it is a big matching -- high matching rate or not, ideally, we would like to see 100 per cent matching rate. This is, of course, the purpose of any matching. Well, whether it is possible to achieve 100 per cent of matches in a certain source, I believe, yes, it is. If there is a good system of individual, unique identification numbers, then, yes, it is. Of course there will be always a small group of records that are deficient in some way, just human errors or something like that that cannot be matched, but we can achieve a matching rate in principle close to 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, let me --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In excellent sources. In excellent sources, not necessarily in sources used in human emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just so this is clear, are you saying that 80 per cent of the names found on the combined voter register were individually matched to a name appearing in the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: 80 per cent of the names found on the combined voters register were matched with the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that number of matched names, then, is that the 142.204 people you've described?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, regarding the method of matching, I was just about to speak about it. In the former Yugoslavia there was a system of individual identification numbers available. These -- the so-called jedinski [phoen], well, individual identification JMBG numbers were introduced around the year 1980 in the former Yugoslavia, and for all those born after this year, 1980, were received -- were issued at birth. For the older population these numbers were issued subsequently at different occasions but there was a deadline, at which, I think in the second half of the'80s, at which the population was to acquire these numbers. In the population census, the JMBG number is available. It is not 100 per cent correct and not 100 per cent available for all individuals. But the JMBG was the basis for our matching of the census with the voters registration. Basis, but we also used other criteria, additional criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to come back to question by Mr. Springer which has prompted Mr. Karnavas to his feet. 80 per cent. We now know what 100 per cent would be, but if you compare your study with comparable studies, is it something to be expected, is it better than expected, is it lower than expected. To what extent does it affect the reliability of the results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very good matching rate. We have been matching sources since 1998 in this unit, and we've been matching all kinds of sources, always with the population census, and the 80 per cent matching rate is a very good matching rate. Only in a few more cases, perhaps one, two, we obtained a matching rate higher than 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, your question wasn't answered. I mean, compared to what? With her studies? But the way I read your question was on outside matters, not just within the OTP. 80 per cent may suffice for her, because she's a member of the OTP, paid by the OTP, employed by the OTP but in comparison to outside is that an acceptable standard of 20 per cent variance, plus or minus. I think -- that's what I thought you wanted the answer to and I don't think she answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me supplement the question. Witness, you stated that you made a comparison to the level of 80 per cent of the registers vote. This total of 80 per cent leaves 20 per cent we don't know anything about. Is that approach, is that work method compatible with a standard applied the world over in your field, and furthermore, when you have an 80 per cent matching rate, can you deem the result to be reliable in terms of international standards? And I'm not talking about the standards applied at the OTP. I believe that you're perfectly capable of answering this question, which is quite straightforward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Well, thank you for the question. I must say I am perhaps alone here at the OTP in doing this work. I have myself at my unit, of course, for these kind of issues, but I'm lucky to have been in touch with several other experts working in the field, including great people like Helge Brunborg, Patrick Ball, who are also experts and presented their reports here. I also worked with other experts, recently with Mr. Philip Verwimp. We had a joint project which I presented earlier today in which we made an assessment of a very exceptional source on casualties of the Bosnian war. I don't think that there is a problem here with this matching rate 80 per cent. I certainly can tell you that this is a generally very good matching rate for this kind of work and for these sources. Of course, there are methods to increase the matching rate, but we've been conservative with matching sources because it's better to undermatch sources than to overmatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering my question. What I would like to know is the following: Is this 80 per cent rate compatible with methods used by other experts? You've named a number of experts. Is it compatible with the methods used in other countries where the same methodology is applied and where it is thought that a rate of 80 per cent, a figure of 80 per cent is a reliable figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we speak of research into consequences of conflict, and I don't think it is -- that it is -- we are speaking of a situation that is not a huge research field in the sense that I could present you here with 10 comparable studies to the study that I'm discussing here. This work is exceptional, the work I'm presenting here. It's exceptional and people follow our example, other people working in the field. So what I'm trying to say, the most of the existing experience comes from this office, and I can compare the results in this project I obtained in very many other projects, and at the same time I know this method has been used by several other experts I know personally, with whom I even worked, and they use this approach the way we do it, and we are all aware of problems when applying this approach, and we apply similar solutions to these problems. And as I said, it's possible to increase the matching rate by using statistical techniques, but then we run the risk that wrong records are mapped. I believe that there is a limit when a match can be declared a true match and this limit cannot be crossed because the risk of making an error when declaring two wrong matches a good match is too high. It's better not to increase the matching rate by statistical method and computer algorithms but better stick to results that are very reliable and at the same time offer a very good matching rate, 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the employee of the Office of the Prosecution has refused to answer the question concretely and directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, Witness, to my question that was extremely specific you responded that the work you conducted is rather -- is unique, because the consequences of a conflict on a given population is a unique type of work that to your knowledge only the OTP was able to conduct in relation to the former Yugoslavia. As a result of this, you are not in a position to compare your work could work accomplished on other conflicts because according to you the work you have done is unique. Is it really what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think what is really unique is the scale of the analysis. I don't think that I could give you examples, other examples of other research groups who would conduct the matching of the census data with another large source like the voters register. I cannot give you these kind of examples. So the scale is absolutely unique. But not the method as such. I can give more examples of the matching done between sources of smaller scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to take a break now. We'll resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The hearing is resumed. Before we bring the witness in, let me read a short oral decision related to the admissibility of exhibits related to witness who testified on the 15th of March, 2007. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit Exhibit P 09882 under seal, as well as P 02732. These exhibits had been submitted by the Prosecution through list IC 00492. They have been admitted since they have a certain probative value and certain relevance. The Trial Chamber most that the Defence has not requested the admission of any exhibits. Let's have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, there's no objection to her hearing any part of this, I would like to make an oral application in the interests of saving time that the Trial Chamber dispense with any further evidence from this witness. There is a basic requirement in the case of an expert witness that there should be at least some degree of scientific comparison and validity to the scientific methodology which is being used --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Mr. President, do believe that this is an argument that should take place out of the hearing of the witness. Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm in the Chamber's hands. I have no objection to the witness hearing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer will proceed with the examination-in-chief, and he will deal again with the methods used for comparison purposes. That will shed some light on the matter. Having said that, Mr. Murphy, this witness has already testified many times here in this Tribunal. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you were getting questions from me and then subsequently counsel and then -- and then the Trial Chamber itself about the 80 per cent matching issue. What I want to do is to take it one step beyond that and maybe that will shed light on the 80 per cent issue. And we're looking at the same slide again as we were before, and I'm looking at the second-to-last point in which you say as a -- the total number of linked or matched individuals for the eight municipalities came to 142.204. You see that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, my question is whether that number of individuals, that number of cases, 142.204, whether that provided you with a large enough sample --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- in which to conduct your studies and particularly whether it's a large enough sample within the standards that would prevail in your profession.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Certainly it is. It is a sample which is approximately 46 per cent of the census population from these eight municipalities, and it's a large sample and as such it can be safely used in the analysis. I want to comment on this 80 per cent as well if I may. Well, the 80 per cent should be seen in the broader perspective of our work, of our project. It wasn't our goal to achieve complete numbers of displaced persons and refugees because that is impossible. Through matching, what could be achieved and has been achieved in this project is the minimum number of the displaced persons and refugees. So if the matching rate could have been 100 per cent, our statistics on the displacement could have been better, higher numbers. They are based on 80 per cent matching rate and they are minimum numbers, but they are coming from a very good sample. In addition to them, to the minimum numbers, we produce more complete numbers based on the statistical estimation, and I think we will discuss these numbers later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I want things to be very clear. There's no problem as far as I'm concerned, but apparently it's not the case for everyone, but at paragraph 5 on the screen you're saying that the vast majority of individuals included in the voters register were matched with individuals found in the 1991 population census. When I read that sentence on the screen in English, it leads me to think that you and your associates went through the voters registers and you took note of the fact that amongst the people who had voted 80 per cent were to be found in the 1991 population census, and the 20 per cent difference might be either new voters or people who had not been registered as part of the 1991 population census. Is that the way you assess this 80 per cent figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 80 per cent the matching rate which relates to the registered voters. 80 per cent of the registered voters have been matched with the census. The registered voters is not a complete population and it has nothing to do with the 20 per cent unmatched records. Those voters who are not in the register simply are not there because they didn't register, and there is another group which is not in the voters register. This is population younger than 18 years. So it is per se a sample, right, of the 1997, 1998 population, the voters register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, have you understood? Is it clear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
